title: TB9-21388
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), claims to be a citizen of Nepal. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the decision of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

The Appellant alleges that he is a long-time member of the Nepali Congress (NC) political party and prior to that he was a member of the NC affiliated student organization called the Nepal Student's Union (NSU) while in school. He indicates that due to his active involvement he has been targeted, extorted, and threatened over the years by Maoists. First, by the Maoists student union and later after he joined and began to support the NC more vocally, he encountered problems with the Youth Communist League (YCL) and most recently with the Biplev Maoists. Particularly, during elections.
He fears he will be harmed or killed by the Maoists if returned to Nepal.
At his RPD hearing on July 22, 2019, he was found not to be a Convention Refugee or Person in Need of protection, and the determinative issue was credibility.

The standard of review is correctness as established in Huruglica1, where the Federal Court of Appeal gives guidance in regard to the role of the RAD. The RPD will defer to findings of the RPD where the RPD has a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral testimony. ANALYSIS Memorandum of Appeal

The determinative issue on appeal is credibility. The Appellant argues that the RAD erred: a. in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility b. in its assessment of the Appellant's documentary evidence

The Appellant is not relying on any new evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and he does not request an oral hearing under ss. 110(6) of the IRPA. Findings related to credibility Knowledge of the Nepali Congress Political Party

The RAD finds that the RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant did not display knowledge of his political party commensurate to someone with the longstanding involvement and membership as alleged.

The RPD found it unreasonable that the Appellant could not explain in a more substantive, detailed, or specific manner, what his party stood for or any specific policies they have implemented and therefore drew a negative inference regarding his credibility.

The Appellant submits that it was an error to find that he was lacking knowledge of his political party given that he testified about characteristics and ideologies of his party, he mentioned that they implemented the new constitution and provided some examples of social policies of the NC party. Further, he submits that the details he gave about his party were correct, the Member did not provide any examples of such polices of programs in her reasons and the hearing is not a memory test nor should his responses be viewed through a subjective/western lens.

The RAD has reviewed the audio recording of the hearing. In his testimony the Appellant indicated that he is of interest to the Maoists because he is an active member of the NC political party and a businessman. He testified that he advocates for Nepali people to join his political party and supports them "during election time to cast vote in favour of Nepali Congress party." He testified that he has formally been a member of the NC since XXXX 2007 and prior to that from 1998-2005 he was a part of their student union. He testified that he chose to support the party because they are democratic and they believe in human rights. When asked what else the party believes in or stands for he testified that from the very beginning they have always advocated for democracy, they are the only party that works for the people, and believe in human rights and he reiterated that they work for the Nepali people. He testified that Sher bahadur Deuba is the leader of the NC and when asked how long he was the leader, the Appellant testified that now he's the president after the last president was expired. He was asked why the party was important to him and he testified that they always work for the people and for the grass roots of Nepal. When asked about any further connection he has to the party, he testified that he used to discuss the present political situation with the NC Cadres.

He was asked later in testimony to talk about any policies which the NC has implemented which he finds commendable or he supports. His reply was "nationalism, federalism and socialism." The member asked whether there was a specific policy; something more practical that the NC had proposed or implemented. He responded that the NC is a very old and big political party, and only after they led the government did Nepal get a new constitution. He testified that the NC led the government since 2013 as they won the second constitutional assembly election in 2013 and went on to give a new constitution in 2015. The member indicated that the constitution is very broad and asked whether there was any kind of social policy or HR related policy that was either proposed or implemented by the NC that he supports. He replied they always advocate for equality and whenever the Nepali people have problems, the NC always wants to support and make the government benefit the people.

The RAD finds that his testimony was extremely vague and lacking in detail. The Appellant was not an average supporter and has indicated that the Maoists are after him based on the fact that he is an active NC member. He was a part of the NSU since 1998, then became a member of the NC. For the 2008 elections he decided to become more involved in the election campaign, according to his evidence he was nominated as the NC campaign XXXX XXXX XXXX for his village. Subsequently, in 2017 his party assigned him to work as the election campaign XXXX for his village which XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Appellant testified that he personally went door to door with other NC members/cadres to request that voters cast their vote in favour of the NC.

The RAD agrees that the hearing is not a memory test, however the RAD finds that the Appellant's knowledge of the party does not align with his alleged political activities and the duration of his membership in the party. His answers about what the party stands for were very general despite being given multiple opportunities to respond. While he named some of their ideologies, he did not explain anything about their views. And, while he argues in the memorandum that he did talk about some policies, the RAD finds that he did not talk about any particular policies aside from the implementation of the constitution. While correct that the constitution was implemented as he described, this is something that anyone living in the country would have knowledge of given its significance at the time. He was also able to name the party leader, but the RAD notes that he never did provide specifics about how long that person has been the leader. Essentially his response was that the current leader became leader after the previous one. The RAD finds that his answers were extremely brief, repetitive and lacking in the level of detail that would reasonably be expected from someone who was most recently a campaign coordinator for the NC and was going door to door in order to ask for people's votes. If one is an advocate for a political party, they should be able to explain what the party stands for or does for the people in more concrete terms.

The Appellant argues that the member did not provide any examples of the policies and programs that it anticipated he would know and also that such policies and programs are not in the National Documentation Package (NDP), it is not the member's onus to establish the claim. Part of the member's role is to evaluate the credibility of a person's testimony, and testimony can be evaluated based on a number of factors including its content, quality and spontaneity. While details of individual policies or programs of the NC may not appear in the NDP, a person's ability to testify about things they personally believe, things they have done or experienced are all relevant considerations particularly where this is the reason they are being pursued. In this case, the member asked open ended questions such as, "Can you tell me about any policies which they have implemented which you find commendable or you support?" There is nothing wrong with asking such questions to get an understanding of the Appellant's specific circumstances.

The Appellant also submits that the member viewed political participation in Nepal through a western lens or in a subjective manner. However, the RAD does not find that to be the case. The Appellant in this case has completed high school, he completed two years of university/college studies, he worked in Nepal and has travelled internationally in the past. Hence, the RAD finds he is fairly sophisticated. Again, if one is an advocate for a political party in any country, they should be able to explain what the party stands for or does for the people in more concrete terms, even if it is done in simple language. However, the RAD finds that his testimony was devoid of any details of what the party actually does. The RAD finds that this significantly undermines the credibility of his account. Treatment of documentary evidence related to his political affiliation

The RAD finds that the RPD did not err in its assessment of the documentary evidence related to his political affiliation. The RAD finds that the RPD was correct in placing no weight on these documents as they are fraudulent.

The RPD found that based on the findings related to the Appellant's credibility and based on the objective documents, which state that fraudulent documents are easily accessible in Nepal, that little weight could be put on the supporting documentary evidence supplied by the Appellant.
The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by ignoring the documentary evidence that he provided in support of his claim without any valid reasons.

In evidence, the Appellant submitted an NC membership card as well as a letter from the NC.2 The RAD has conducted its own independent analysis and has examined the membership card. The RAD notes that it has no date of issuance on it. It does however have dates and signatures reflecting when renewals occurred; in 2009 and 2014, respectively on the back page of the card. The description provided on the back page says that the Appellant has been "following and internalizing with discipline ideology, Nationality, Democracy Socialism according to the constitution of the Nepali Congress 2017 (1960 AD) (Amended and Refined) ..." The RAD finds that membership could not have been issued under the constitution of 2017 prior to that year. Therefore, the renewal dates on this card reflecting the years 2009 and 2014 do not accord with the chronology as one cannot renew a card in 2009 and 2014 that refers to a constitution with a future date.

The RAD finds on a balance of probabilities that this document submitted by the Appellant is fraudulent and the RAD finds that the Appellant's submission of a fraudulent document in support of his case damages his credibility.

The letter, allegedly from the same organization; the NC speaks generally about the fact that he has been associated with the party for a long time, but he had to leave the country after the Biplav Maoists made extortion demands, asked that he quit the NC party and attacked him physically. The letter indicates that he supported them during the elections in 2008 and 2013, and during the elections in 2017. The RAD notes that the letter is very general in that it makes no reference to the fact that he was the NC campaign XXXX XXXX XXXX in 2008, nor to the fact that the party assigned him to work as the election campaign XXXX in Purunchuar in 2017, which the panel finds unusual as he had duties beyond that of a normal member. And, the letter talks about his support in 2013 when this is not something that the Appellant talked about himself in either his Basis of Claim (BOC) or his testimony.

The RAD notes that as per case law, submitting a false or irregular document may have an impact on the weight assigned to other documents provided by the Appellant, especially when they are interrelated,3 and on the overall credibility of an Appellant.4 The RAD finds that given the use of a fraudulent membership card, that no weight can be put on this letter or on the press release, which was allegedly issued by the same organization.

These documents were expressly proffered to illustrate that the Appellant is an active member of this political party who is wanted by the Maoists based on his political activities. Given that the membership card is fraudulent, and the Appellant's testimony about his political party lacked credibility, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is not a member of the NC as alleged and he is not being sought for that reason as alleged. Knowledge of his father's political activities
The RAD finds that the RPD was incorrect to draw a negative inference from the Appellant's lack of knowledge about his father's political activities.
The RPD found that it was unreasonable that the Appellant could not recall any specific memories of his father's involvement with the political party and drew a negative inference.

The Appellant argues that it was an error to draw a negative inference from his lack of knowledge about his father's involvement in the party. He argues that the panel member failed to give examples of what a very active NC member ought to do and as such, the member's conclusion is not reasonable and he should be believed.

At the hearing, the Appellant confirmed that his father was a very active member of the NC. When asked about what his father's involvement was, the Appellant testified that he was a member of the NC party and was involved in the NC politics. When asked if he could explain anything more, he testified that his father always helped the NC party in the village where they lived and he advocated about the NC policy and drove membership in their village. When asked to tell the member about a specific memory about him being involved in the NC, he testified that he could not remember.

The RAD finds that while a person may know generally about another person, they cannot necessarily be expected to know or recall details of someone else's day to day activities. Further, there is no indication that his father was anything more than a general member of the party. Had he held some type of position in the party, it may have been more reasonable to expect that his father's activities would be memorable. The RAD finds it was an error to draw a negative inference from the Appellant's inability to name a specific memory of his father's involvement in the NC. Contradictory evidence regarding his role in the Nepali Student Union

The RAD finds that the RPD was correct to draw a negative inference from his failure to mention his role in the Nepali Student Union (NSU). The RPD found that a contradiction between his narrative and testimony regarding his role in the NSU, detracted from his credibly.
The Appellant argues that it was an error to find that there was an inconsistency between his testimony and his BOC regarding his involvement in the NSU regarding running for the student election.

The Appellant's testimony at the hearing was that he was actively involved in the student union from 1998 to 2006. He testified that while at the XXXX XXXX campus and later at a private college he was involved in the student union and whenever there were activities called by the NC he used to participate. He testified that he also used to participate in the NSU programs on campus. For example, they would intervene when there were problems related to the students, such as hikes in tuition fees or in the price of transportation which affected the students. He testified that the student union would get together with the concerned authorities and discuss these matters. He testified that in the executive body of the student union there were twelve members including himself who were like representatives/leadership of the NSU. He was asked why he did not mention in his narrative that he was one of the leaders of the NSU, but rather the narrative indicates that NSU leaders asked him to contest for student union elections on behalf of the NSU, but due to a conflict with Maoists he did not take that opportunity. He responded that he only mentioned that he was involved with the student union when studying in college and he did not think that he had to mention everything so he may have missed that one.

Counsel questioned the Appellant further about his time on the Executive committee. He confirmed that he was one of the twelve persons appointed to that committee while he was studying in college. He testified that first he became a member of the NSU and then he was on the Executive committee, but he was threatened by the Maoists affiliated student union.

The BOC narrative5 indicates: I was approached by the NSU leaders and asked me to contest in the Student Union elections on behalf of NSU. It was a great moment for me. However, the Maoist's affiliated revolutionary student's union threatened me not to participate in the election representing NSU. Due to arguments and clashes with the Maoists affiliated students, I could not grab that opportunity.

The RAD finds that rather than a contradiction, this was an omission. The RAD finds that there may have been a misunderstanding as it appears that during testimony the Appellant was using NSU and student union interchangeably. To the RAD it appears that his oral evidence was solely with respect to his participation in the NSU. However, this still leaves the issue of being part of the executive committee of the NSU.

While he did indicate in his narrative that he was actively involved in NSU activities, he failed to mention that he actually had a leadership role within that organization, such that it brought him to the attention of and put him in direct conflict to the Maoists. The RAD finds that his explanation; that he did not think he had to mention everything is not reasonable. Had he been a prominent member of the NSU having been on the Executive committee, this is something that should have been mentioned in his narrative.

Contrary to the Appellants arguments, the RAD finds that it is not a foregone conclusion that someone who is a leader of the NSU would run for student union elections. He also argues that he had different interpreters, however, the Appellant signed the BOC form to indicate that the contents of his BOC and attached narrative were true, complete and correct, and he verified that the signature was his at the outset of the hearing.

He also argues that this is not central to the claim because it happened some 15-20 years ago and it should not impugn his credibility. However, the RAD finds that this is a significant detail. He indicates that he has historically had issues with Maoists due to his activities on behalf of the NS. Clearly, he remembered the detail at the hearing, which is arguably a more stressful setting. Had he been in this role, the RAD finds that it is not something that he would easily have forgotten and the RAD finds that this further undermines the credibility of his account. Subjective fear

The RAD finds that the RPD was correct in its finding regarding subjective fear. The RPD found that the Appellant did not reasonably explain his nearly two-month delay in leaving Nepal while he allegedly feared persecution and drew a negative inference. She found that his behavior was indicative of a lack of subjective fear.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by finding he lacked subjective fear due to his delay in departure from the country. He submits that his explanation should have been accepted as reasonable given that he was living in a different city, he had changed his number and was living a low profile.

At the hearing the Appellant verified that his Canadian visa was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2018, but he did not depart the country until XXXX XXXX, 2018. He testified that despite being fearful of the Maoists and living in hiding he waited to leave because he had applied to participate in a particular program, and he believed if he travelled to Canada earlier that Immigration might not allow him into the country. He testified that he got that information from the Agency who helped process his visa. He confirmed also that he had a valid multiple entry visa in his possession, but having heard about the Trump administration and its policies he thought he could live peacefully in Canada so he made the decision to come to Canada instead. He was asked why he did not go to the United States (US) first at least temporarily and then come to Canada after his program began. He testified in response that he had applied for his wife also as he wanted them to come together, but her visa was rejected. He testified that he found out in the first week of February that she had been refused.

The RAD finds that it is not that the RPD failed to consider his explanation, but rather the RPD found that the explanation was not reasonable in the circumstances. The RAD finds while his explanation for the delay until February is reasonable given he had hoped to travel with his wife, the subsequent delay after that point is not. He found out in early February that his wife would not be able to go with him and he had no indication of if/when she would be able to travel. As he was the one at risk, the RAD finds that it would have been reasonable to depart at that time or shortly thereafter given that he had the means to do so with his US visa. While the US may not have been his final destination, had he been fearful that the Maoists could find him anywhere in Nepal, each day that he remained in the country would have meant a further unnecessary risk to his life. The RAD finds that this delay does undermine the credibility of his account and illustrates a lack of subjective fear. Documentary evidence
The RAD finds that the RPD did not err in its findings regarding the corroborative documents.

The Appellant argues that the member erred by rejecting the corroborative documentary evidence that he submitted in support of his claim without having evidence to discredit them. He submits that the availability of forged documents should not be a reason to conclude that his documents are fraudulent as per caselaw. Further, he submits that the RPDs finding that threat letters are not being issued to individuals is based on a selective reading of the objective documents and other items in the NDP, which indicate the opposite were ignored.

The RAD has done its own independent assessment. The RAD finds that the remainder of the documents can be given no weight based on the credibility findings outlined above and because objective documents indicate that fraudulent documents are easy to obtain, and most importantly given his submission of fraudulent documents from the NC in support of his claim as discussed above. Given he is not a member of the NC and not being pursued for that reason, documents that say otherwise are not authentic.

There is a Response to Information Request (RIR) on the subject of false documents titled; Nepal: Prevalence and availability of fraudulent documents such as police certificates and reports, medical reports or hospital records, employment records and certificates (2014- June 2016). It outlines the following: In correspondence with the Research Directorate, the Nepal researcher for the Asian Human Rights Commission (AHRC), an independent Hong Kong-based NGO "which seeks to promote greater awareness and realization of human rights in the Asian region" (AHRC n.d.), provided the opinion that "forgery of documents is big business" in Nepal (ibid. 29 June 2016)...the same source indicated that if an individual is aware of "the proper channel" and can offer "adequate money," documents can "easily" be forged or bought (ibid). The Researcher also stated that in Nepal "you can easily design a letterhead [or] stamp for less than [US$]5" (ibid.). According to the source, in addition to police reports, medical and hospital records and reports, and employment records and certificates, forged documents also include citizenship certificates, passports and driver's licenses (ibid.).6

The RAD has reviewed this RIR in its entirety and finds that unlike what is argued by the Appellant, there are multiple sources that confirm the availability of fraudulent documents in the country and discuss various examples or instances of arrest for production of fake documents. The sources include the aforementioned Asian Human Rights Commission (AHRC), a lawyer from a Kathmandu based law firm, newspaper The Himalayan Times, the US Department of State's Trafficking in Persons Report June 2016, The US Department of State's Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 2015, newspaper Republica, and the Canadian Consulate in Kathmandu. Hence, it is not only the lawyer whose information they appear to question in the memorandum that supplied this information.

In fact, the RAD finds that the Appellant engaged in a selective reading of the NDP as he drew his information from one section; the second section with a subtitle Fraudulent or Forged Police Certificates and Reports. He accurately points out that the Canadian consulate in Kathmandu says they were not aware of the availability of fraudulent or forged police certificates in Nepal, while the lawyer indicates such police certificates are common. However, this is in relation to the one type of document only; police certificates. The RAD notes that in the other sections on medical and hospital records, and employment and education records, the Canadian consulate confirms they are aware of the availability of these types of fraudulent documents. The RAD finds that all sections of the RIR must be considered. As multiple reliable sources confirm that fraudulent documents are widely available and two of those sources specifically mention the production of fraudulent police documents, the RAD finds that police certificates can be forged.

With respect to the arguments related to whether or not the Maoists are issuing threat letters currently, the RAD finds it is not necessary to address this given that it would not change the outcome of the Appeal. Circumstances of the Appellant

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by making credibility findings without giving special consideration to his circumstances. He argues that in the Board's own publication titled Assessment of Credibility in Claims for Refugee Protection, it outlines that psychological condition, age, cognitive difficulties, the passage of time, gender considerations, the claimant's educational background, social position and cultural factors should be considered. He argues that the RPD focused on testing his memory rather than on the persecution he faced and that it focused on events that occurred twenty years ago when he was young, it did not consider his cultural and language background, or that he underwent traumatic incidents.

The RAD finds that the RPD did not engage in a memory test. The Member asked questions about the political party that the Appellant belonged to, which was the source of his problems and why he was targeted by the opposing political party. The questions were generally open ended and allowed the Appellant to describe things in his own words such as "Why did you choose to support that party in particular?" And, "give me a specific example of something you did as a member of the Nepali student union?" Having reviewed the audio recording of the hearing, the RAD finds that the RPDs questions were driven by incidents that the Appellant wrote about in his BOC, and the RPD asked questions about both older and newer incidents, so there was no particular emphasis on the older ones as the Appellant suggests.

While he indicates that his cultural and language background were not taken into account, he fails to indicate how this happened and where an error resulted. A Nepali interpreter was used at the hearing to translate all questions and answers, and when he misunderstood things, questions were rephrased or put to him again so he had the opportunity to express himself in his language of choice. And, while he indicates that he underwent trauma, there is no indication that the member was insensitive or asked inappropriate questions. The RAD finds no indication that the RPD did not give due consideration to the Appellant's particular circumstances. Other arguments

The Appellant made other arguments in relation to the RPDs credibility assessment; that the credibility findings were vague and based on unreasonable and irrelevant considerations without regard for the corroborative evidence. That the reasons for disbelieving him were not clear, and that microscopic findings were made.
The RAD finds it unnecessary to address this as the RAD has conducted its own independent assessment above and articulated the reasons for disbelieving his allegations clearly. Credibility conclusion

The Appellant argued that a number of incidents occurred at various points with the Maoists, their youth group, the YCL and most recently a breakaway faction of the Maoists known as the Biplav Maoists. However, the underlying reason for these attacks was his political profile. The RAD finds that he is not credible regarding that political profile given his lack of knowledge of the NC, the significant omission about his role in the NSU, his demonstrated lack of subjective fear and his submission of false documents in support of his claim. As such, the RAD finds that the lack of credibility extends to the balance of his allegations and that on a balance of probabilities the events did not occur as alleged.

Based on all of the above, and on the RAD's own assessment of the evidence including the audio recording, the supporting documents, and the objective evidence, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not established on a balance of probabilities that he is at risk in Nepal
The RAD finds the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD and dismisses the appeal. (signed) "T. Andrews" T. Andrews October 24, 2019 Date 1 M.C.I. v.
